verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.2 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate. Viṣaya is 'sense-objects'; 'objects of craving' is a fair gloss. Tāta ('dear child') as 'my son' is fine.
context: This is the opening of the dialogue. King Janaka has just asked three questions in 1.1: how knowledge, liberation and dispassion are gained. This is Ashtavakra's first reply, and from 1.3 he turns straight to the teaching that Janaka is the witnessing consciousness, not the elements.

key_terms.sense: treat sense-objects, and the pull toward them, as poison
forbearance, forgiveness as an inner quality
straightness; mind and speech in agreement
take in, cultivate, as if it were nectar

core_teaching: Freedom starts with two practices together: loosening the grip of sense-objects, and actively cultivating forbearance, honesty, kindness, contentment and truthfulness, which purify the mind for self-knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Shunning objects means dropping the 'this is mine' attachment born of identifying with body and mind, plus sense-control. The virtues purify the mind: non-attachment is the negative half of practice, virtue the positive. Cites Ramakrishna on sincerity and truth.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Objects can't literally be abandoned while the body lives; obsessive attachment is what goes. Be content with what prarabdha brings, don't lie or grovel to get things, see their faults. He mocks nakedness and begging as false renunciation.

practical_reading: In daily life it works as a two-step practice: notice what hooks you and hold it at arm's length, and deliberately practise patience, honesty, kindness, contentment and truthfulness.
misreadings: Not a call to reject all pleasures or possessions; Jalim Singh says objects are still used, and it is the attachment that goes
Forgiveness (kṣamā) is forbearance grown inside, not a duty to put up with ongoing harm
Not a moral checklist that earns freedom; in the text it prepares the mind for self-knowledge
cautions: 'Poison' language about desire can feed shame in someone struggling with appetite, addiction or body image. Frame it as loosening a grip, not as self-disgust.
speaks_to: Someone feeling pulled around by cravings, shopping, scrolling or habits
A person wanting a concrete first step in inner work
Someone rebuilding trust after dishonesty who wants to practise truthfulness
not_for: A person being pressured to 'forgive' an abuser
Someone with an eating disorder or compulsive guilt about desire, if read as 'desire is poison'

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.4 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: This is part of Ashtavakra's opening reply. In 1.3 he tells Janaka that he is none of the five elements but the consciousness that witnesses them. This verse states the result of resting as that witness: happiness, peace and freedom, right now.

key_terms.sense: setting the body apart, seeing yourself as distinct from it

core_teaching: Freedom is not a distant goal. It follows at once from no longer identifying with the body and abiding as consciousness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The essence of Advaita practice. Identifying with the body loads its birth, ageing, disease and death onto the Self. Drop that and you know yourself as consciousness at once; body and mind only hide it, as clouds hide the sun.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Bondage lasts only while the 'knot' of mutual superimposition between consciousness and the inert mind remains; as heated iron seems to burn, the Self seems to act. Cut the knot and freedom is immediate; moksha is not elsewhere.

practical_reading: It can be used as a pause practice: step back, notice the body and its sensations as things you are aware of, and rest in that awareness for a few breaths.
misreadings: Not a dissociation technique or a denial of bodily needs or pain
'Right now' is a claim about the Self, not a promise that problems vanish instantly
cautions: For someone with dissociation, depersonalisation or trauma, 'set the body apart' can be destabilising; grounding in the body may be what they need
speaks_to: Someone over-identified with appearance, ageing or illness
Anxious people who need a felt moment of calm
Seekers who think freedom is far away
not_for: People experiencing dissociation or depersonalisation
Someone with a new serious diagnosis who needs their body taken seriously

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.5 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Translation accurate. The line's 'what others can see' shifts akṣagocara ('an object of the senses/eye') toward how others see you; it is a modern gloss, not the verse's point.
context: Continuing the opening instruction, after saying Janaka is not the elements (1.3), Ashtavakra strips away social and perceptual identities: caste, stage of life, anything the eye can see. Next (1.6) he says merit and demerit, pleasure and pain belong to the mind.

key_terms.sense: belonging to one of the four stages of life
an object of the senses or eye

core_teaching: The Self has none of the labels that society or perception give it. It is the unattached, formless witness, and knowing this is the basis of happiness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Āśrama means the four stages of life. The Self is never an object of sense-knowledge, so neither caste nor āśrama can be said of it, and the Self as such has no obligation to perform the duties tied to them.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: One consciousness appears divided, as space does in many pots, untouched by the dust in them. When Janaka objects that dropping varna-ashrama duties is sinful, Ashtavakra replies that those duties are for the ignorant, not the knower.

practical_reading: It can loosen an identity built on status, caste, job title or stage of life: what you are underneath is the one who sees all these roles.
misreadings: Not a social programme against caste, though it is often quoted against caste pride; its claim is about the Self
Not licence to drop duties while one still identifies with the body; Jalim Singh's answer concerns the knower
cautions: Caste is a live and painful subject. Avoid implying that discrimination does not matter because 'you are not your caste'.
Jalim Singh's tika says varna duties are for the ignorant; don't present that as the verse's plain meaning.
speaks_to: Someone feeling reduced to a label such as caste, job, age or marital status
A person in a life transition (retirement, empty nest) whose role has changed
not_for: Someone facing caste discrimination, if it sounds like 'just transcend it'

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.8 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: The translation is accurate. The line and misuse note change 'I am not the doer' into 'not the ONLY doer'. Both commentators deny doership to the Self entirely (the body-mind acts). It works as pastoral advice, but readings should not attribute 'only' to the verse.
context: Ashtavakra has just said (1.6–1.7) that merit and demerit, pleasure and pain belong to the mind, and that Janaka is the one seer, neither doer nor enjoyer. Here the doer-sense is pictured as a snakebite. In 1.9 the next step is to burn the forest of ignorance with the conviction 'I am pure awareness'.

key_terms.sense: bitten by the great black cobra
nectar of faith or firm conviction

core_teaching: The conviction 'I am the doer' is a poison that binds. The antidote is a firm conviction that the Self does not act; body and mind do.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: It is a black serpent because egoism brings spiritual death. The nectar revives and removes pain: in the same way, destroying egoism revives spiritual awareness and frees one from worldly misery.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The conceit 'I do this and will enjoy its fruit' is the black snake whose bite keeps the whole world in birth and death. Only the firm conviction 'I am not the doer' cures it; nothing else brings happiness.

practical_reading: It applies to over-responsibility and control. Notice the inner claim 'everything depends on me', do your part, and let outcomes rest with the larger web of causes.
misreadings: Not an excuse to avoid accountability for one's actions
The verse denies doership to the Self altogether; it is not a teamwork message about sharing the load
cautions: Our line softens the doctrine. Fine as application, but say so if quoting the verse itself.
speaks_to: Managers or parents carrying everything on themselves
not_for: Someone avoiding responsibility for harm they caused
Someone who already feels powerless, since it could deepen helplessness

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.11 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Yā matiḥ sā gatiḥ' is literally 'as the conviction, so the destination'.
context: After telling Janaka that he is the ever-free witness, Ashtavakra quotes a popular saying. The next verse (1.12) says the Self only seems to be caught in samsara, through error.

key_terms.sense: one who takes oneself to be free
one who takes oneself to be bound
as the conviction, so the outcome or destination

core_teaching: The Self is always free, so bondage lasts only through the conviction of being bound. Holding the conviction of freedom dissolves it.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self never really enters bondage. Our thought that we are bound keeps the bondage going. Thinking constantly of oneself as the free Self removes the binding thought, and one finds one was always free.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Bondage comes from identification (abhimāna) like 'I am a brahmin, a kshatriya', which drives action, fruits and rebirth. One who knows 'I am pure, formless, ever free' is free. He ties the saying to one's final thought shaping one's end.

practical_reading: It helps you notice self-limiting stories ('I'm stuck', 'I'm broken') and practise identifying with what is free in you, while still dealing with real problems.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking' or manifesting outcomes
Does not mean that external constraints such as illness, poverty or oppression are imaginary or self-caused
cautions: Can be misheard as blaming people for their suffering ('you're bound because you think so'). Use care with depression or oppression.
Jalim Singh's gloss ties it to one's thought at the moment of death; avoid that framing near bereavement.
speaks_to: Someone trapped in a story of being stuck or unworthy
Someone after a setback who has absorbed 'I'm a failure'
not_for: Someone with clinical depression who may hear blame
People facing structural injustice, if framed as a matter of mindset only

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.16 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Toward the end of chapter 1, Ashtavakra piles up images of the Self as the ground of the world (1.10, the snake seen in a rope). This verse says the universe is pervaded by consciousness and strung on it; 1.17 then lists the Self's qualities.

key_terms.sense: strung, woven, like beads on a thread

core_teaching: The Self is the consciousness that pervades and holds the world, so one should not shrink into a petty, limited self-image.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self is the substance of the universe, which cannot exist without it as its ground. 'Small-minded' means thinking of oneself in a way unlike this true nature.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: As gold pervades bangles and clay pervades pots, consciousness pervades the world and strings it like beads. The world's reality is borrowed, like silver seen in mother-of-pearl. He quotes Madalasa's lullaby: you are pure and awake.

practical_reading: It is an invitation to step out of petty reactions such as grudges, comparison and small anxieties by remembering a larger identity.
misreadings: Not grandiosity or ego inflation ('I am everything, so I matter most')
'Pettiness' here means identifying with the limited self, not a moral insult
cautions: Jalim Singh's claim that the world is unreal can feel dismissive to someone in acute loss
speaks_to: Someone stuck in resentment or comparison
Someone who feels small or insignificant
not_for: Someone in mania or grandiosity

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 1.17 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: 'Self-reliant' for nirbhara is not supported. Nityaswarupananda has 'devoid of bulk and form', Richards 'formless', Baijnath (1904) 'ever full'. Suggest 'full' or 'weightless'. Commentators read the first half as a description ('you are...') and only the last word as a command; our all-imperative 'Be...' is acceptable.
context: This is the last of the descriptions of the Self in chapter 1, before 1.18–20 contrast form (unreal) with the formless (permanent) and use the images of a mirror and space in a pot.

key_terms.sense: whose only inclination is toward consciousness

core_teaching: The verse describes the Self, and anyone resting in it, as needing nothing, unchanging, deep and unshaken, and urges holding to consciousness alone.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Cool, because the heat of passion cannot reach the Self. Unfathomable, because consciousness is beyond relative knowledge. Unperturbed by inner or outer events. He reads the verse as telling you what you are, then urging: desire consciousness alone.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Nirapekṣa means free of the six 'waves' (hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, birth, death) and the body's six changes. The Self is their witness, hence changeless and cool, meaning blissful. Be established in consciousness, free of action.

practical_reading: In a heated moment, the verse is a portrait to recall gently: the cool, deep, unshaken witness behind the reaction.
misreadings: Not a demand to suppress emotion or manufacture calm
Not a relational ideal of needing no one
cautions: 'Needing nothing' could be heard as 'don't need anyone' by someone lonely or avoidant
speaks_to: People wanting an image of steadiness
not_for: Someone grieving who would hear 'be cool and unshaken'

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 2.14 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
attribution_note: Speaker Janaka is correct: chapter 2 is Janaka's response.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Chapter 2 is Janaka's ecstatic response to Ashtavakra's teaching. A run of verses (2.11–2.14) begins 'aho aham', 'how wonderful I am'. In the next verse (2.15) he says knower, knowing and known are not ultimately real.

key_terms.sense: whatever speech and mind can reach

core_teaching: Seeing himself as consciousness, Janaka marvels that as an individual he owns nothing, yet as the Self everything that can be spoken of or thought is his.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: 'Nothing' because only the Self exists, or because the unattached Self owns nothing. 'Everything' because the Self projects and supports the universe. 'Speech and mind' marks the phenomenal world, since only phenomena can be named or thought.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Nothing related to me is real; only Brahman is. Whatever mind and speech can reach is unreal and has no real link to the conscious Self, so Janaka bows to his own wondrous Self.

practical_reading: The paradox can be applied to possessiveness: hold nothing as 'mine', and you can meet everything with ease and wonder.
misreadings: 'I bow to myself' is not ego-worship; it is reverence for the Self as consciousness
Not a claim to own the world materially
cautions: Out of context, 'I bow to myself' can sound narcissistic; explain that the speaker is marvelling at consciousness
speaks_to: Someone after a loss of possessions or status who finds unexpected freedom
Moments of awe or joy after an insight
not_for: Someone in grandiosity
Someone who has just lost everything materially and needs practical help, if it sounds glib

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 3.1 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Translation accurate. Sanskrit typo: our text reads 'तवात्मज्ञानस्य'. Both Nityaswarupananda and Jalim Singh read 'तवात्मज्ञस्य', and the extra syllable breaks the metre.
context: This opens chapter 3, 'Test of the disciple's realisation'. After Janaka's exultant chapter 2, Ashtavakra probes whether the realisation is real, pointing out contradictions such as attachment to wealth and sex (3.1–3.8). From 3.9 he describes the true knower.
core_teaching: If you truly know yourself as one and imperishable, the urge to keep piling up wealth should fall away. Continued craving shows the gap between claimed and real understanding.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Janaka is not yet fully established, so Ashtavakra tests him, pointing out anomalies in his behaviour to improve him. A realised person knows himself as perfect and immortal and wants nothing; how could he long for wealth?

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Having examined Janaka's experience, the teacher tests him again. Knowing the Self as free of all limits of time, place and object, why do you still seem to delight in collecting worldly wealth? What is the cause?

practical_reading: It works as a self-check: when your spiritual talk and your spending or acquiring habits don't match, notice it without self-condemnation.
misreadings: Not against earning a living, or against a king managing a treasury; the target is delight (rati) in accumulating
A test aimed at someone claiming realisation, not a blanket condemnation of the wealthy
cautions: Can shame someone anxious about money for legitimate needs
speaks_to: Someone noticing compulsive accumulation or a never-enough feeling
Someone whose stated values and spending don't match
not_for: Someone in financial hardship working to meet basic needs

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 3.3 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate. Dīna is 'wretched, needy'; 'beggar' is acceptable but sharper than the Sanskrit.
context: This is part of Ashtavakra's test of Janaka (3.1–3.8). Verse 3.2 compared craving to greed for 'silver' that is really mother-of-pearl. Here the image is the ocean and its waves; 3.4 turns to sexual attachment.

key_terms.sense: you run about like someone wretched and needy

core_teaching: One who knows himself as the ocean-like ground in which the world arises has no reason to behave like someone in need.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: All fear, misery, helplessness and want come from seeing the universe as other than one's self. As waves are nothing but the sea, the universe is nothing but the Self; such knowledge should make one serene, fearless and self-contained.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Waves appear in the sea without separate reality of their own, and so does the world. One who has realised 'I am the ground of all' does not run toward objects like a poor man driven by thirst.

practical_reading: When you feel a frantic sense of lack, recall the fullness the waves rise from before chasing the next thing.
misreadings: Not contempt for the poor; dīna describes an inner state of neediness
The barb is aimed at someone who claims knowledge, not at someone struggling
cautions: The 'beggar' image can wound someone in real poverty; prefer 'like someone in need'
speaks_to: Frantic striving, fear of missing out, never-enough feelings
Someone who knows spiritual ideas but still feels desperate
not_for: Someone in actual material deprivation

context: After the test verses, from 3.9 Ashtavakra describes the genuine knower. This verse deals with praise and blame; the next deals with fear of death.

key_terms.sense: as if it were someone else's body

core_teaching: One who sees his own body's activity as if it belonged to someone else cannot be shaken by praise or blame aimed at that activity.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Praise and blame always refer to behaviour carried out through body and mind. One who sees bodily and mental activity as unconnected with the Self is unaffected by them. He cites Gita 3.27–28.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Another person's body is a place of activity separate from my Self, and so is my own. The knower who sees this never feels elation at praise or agitation at blame; if he does, he is not yet a knower.

practical_reading: With feedback and criticism, watch your own conduct as a fair observer would, take what is useful, and let the sting pass.
misreadings: Not indifference to feedback or to how one's actions affect others
Not dissociation from one's body
cautions: For someone with depersonalisation, 'see your body as someone else's' can be distressing
speaks_to: Someone hurt by criticism, reviews or social media
not_for: People with dissociation
Someone who needs to take responsibility for harm

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 3.11 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate. 'A mere show' softens māyāmātra ('mere illusion'), but the sense is kept.
context: This is still the portrait of the true knower (3.9–3.14). After praise and blame (3.10), Ashtavakra asks how one who sees the world as illusion could fear death.
core_teaching: One who sees the world as mere appearance and has lost fascination with it cannot be terrified, even as death approaches.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: One cannot be interested in what does not truly exist. The Self is birthless and deathless; birth and death are illusory, so the knower has no reason to fear the body's dissolution. He cites Gita 2.13–18.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The visible world is maya's product and so unreal. The knower who sees this doesn't brood over where bodies come from or go, and isn't afraid as death approaches; if bewildered by it, he is no knower.

practical_reading: It can soften fear of mortality by loosening fascination with worldly drama, best for people facing ageing or illness who are already reflective and steady.
misreadings: Not that life or people don't matter
Not a test in which fearing death means spiritual failure
cautions: Mentions death directly. 'The world is illusion' can feel dismissive in fresh grief or after a terminal diagnosis.
Not for anyone with suicidal thoughts, since 'the world is a mere show' can feed detachment from life
speaks_to: Reflective people facing ageing or mortality with some steadiness already
Anxiety about death in someone not in crisis
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Suicidal ideation
The first days after a terminal diagnosis

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 8.1–8.2. Our Sanskrit and translation contain two ślokas: 8.1 (bondage) and 8.2 (freedom). In Nityaswarupananda, Jalim Singh and Richards, 8.1 is the bondage half only.

translation_note: Translation accurate for both verses. Sanskrit typos in the first half: 'दृष्यति' should be 'हृष्यति' (as in our own second half and in all translators' glosses, 'is pleased'); 'गृण्हाति' should be 'गृह्णाति'.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Freedom is when the mind seeks neither to gain enjoyments nor to shed sorrows: no elation at gain, no grief when loved ones are lost or separated. On 8.3 he adds that once discernment ends attachment, the mind stays free.

practical_reading: It can become a check-in: which of the six movements (wanting, grieving, grabbing, pushing away, elation, anger) is running me right now?
misreadings: Not a rule against feeling; it describes being driven by feelings
Not 'grief is bondage, so stop grieving'
cautions: Grieving is listed as bondage, and Jalim Singh's gloss names not grieving when loved ones die. Never use on Day 1 of a grief plan.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Egoism is bondage because it identifies the Self with body and mind; without ego the Self is known as one without a second. With this knowledge one becomes perfectly tranquil, free of desire and aversion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha

practical_reading: 'Lightly' is the key: instead of straining to drop things, notice the 'I' that grasps and loosen the grip with some playfulness.

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 9.1 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Mostly accurate, with two loose spots. (1) The Sanskrit names two things, 'done and undone' (kṛtākṛte) AND 'the pairs of opposites' (dvandvāni); our version merges them into one. (2) 'Tyāgaparaḥ' is 'intent on letting go / renunciation', not 'become free'.
context: This opens chapter 9, 'Detachment' (nirveda). Jalim Singh says its eight verses set out what dispassion looks like, to steady Janaka's experience. Verses 9.2–9.3 add that it is rare for anyone to lose the urge to live, enjoy and know, and that everything is transient.

key_terms.sense: what is done and not done; duties
pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain

core_teaching: Neither duties nor the pairs of opposites ever come to an end, for anyone. Seeing this, become intent on letting go through disenchantment, free of compulsive vows and observances.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Life mixes joy and sorrow, and preferences create the sense of duty. While the world seems real, opposites and duty never end; the way out is to see its hollowness and renounce. 'Avratī' means desireless, since vows presuppose wanting gain.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: 'Done and undone' is the insistence that this must be done and that must not; the pairs are pleasure and pain. Since these never cease for anyone embodied, don't insist on them: be avratī, holding stubbornly to nothing.

practical_reading: Applied to the endless to-do list: the list never ends, so stop waiting to finish everything before you are at peace, and hold obligations more lightly.
misreadings: Not permission to drop responsibilities

cautions: Nityaswarupananda's note leans toward renouncing the world; for householders, frame it as letting go inwardly
speaks_to: Perfectionists waiting to finish everything before resting
not_for: Someone looking for a reason to abandon dependants

misreadings: Accepting life's swings is not accepting mistreatment
Not fatalism about situations that can be changed

not_for: Someone in an abusive or unsafe situation

not_for: Someone who needs to make an informed decision and might take it as 'all views are equally useless'

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes

Not 'you deserved your misfortune'

not_for: Victims of injustice or abuse

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The preceding verses say suffering comes through karma and is unavoidable. But if we detach the mind when it comes, it will not affect us; dwelling on it intensifies it.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: He uses it to explain how one acts without being bound: here, suffering comes from worry alone. One sure of this drops worry, becomes calm and steady, and though acting does not experience the fruits.

practical_reading: It separates pain from the extra suffering of rumination: deal with the problem, and drop the loop.
misreadings: Not that all suffering is imaginary
Real problems still need attention
cautions: Telling someone with an anxiety disorder 'suffering is only worry' can sound dismissive; pair it with care
not_for: Someone in physical pain or acute crisis
Clinical anxiety, if framed as 'just stop worrying'

attribution_note: Speaker Janaka is correct: chapter 13 is Janaka's.
translation_note: Translation accurate. Sanskrit typo: 'स्वास्थं' should be 'स्वास्थ्यं' (both editions).
context: Chapter 13, 'Happiness', is Janaka's seven-verse song, each verse ending 'I live happily' (yathāsukham). In 13.2 he adds that he has set aside the strains of body, speech and mind.

key_terms.sense: ease; literally being established in oneself

core_teaching: The ease of inwardly having nothing is rare even for the outward renunciate. So Janaka drops both renouncing and acquiring, and lives at ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Svāsthya literally means being established in the Self; this tranquillity is uncaused and inherent. Even a loincloth implies relative consciousness, and renunciation also presupposes ego and attachment, so true happiness lies beyond both.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The steadiness that comes from dropping attachment to all objects does not arise if one is attached even to a loincloth. So the disciple gives up attachment to both renouncing and taking, and rests in the Self's bliss.

practical_reading: It addresses spiritual or minimalist striving: inner ease comes not from owning less or more, but from being driven by neither grabbing nor giving up.
misreadings: Not against simplicity or monastic life
Not 'anything goes' in consumption
speaks_to: Someone caught between consumerism and guilt-driven minimalism
People who renounced outwardly but feel no peace
not_for: Someone whose poverty is not chosen, if 'having nothing' is romanticised

translation_note: Accurate. 'by me' is interpretive; Nityaswarupananda has 'by the Self'.
context: This is from Janaka's song of happiness (chapter 13). After setting aside the strains of body, speech and mind (13.2), here he does what comes without the sense of 'I did it'. Verse 13.4 continues the theme of action and non-action; 18.20 repeats the thought.

key_terms.sense: nothing at all is really done (by the Self)
whatever comes up to be done

core_teaching: Knowing that in truth the Self does nothing, Janaka simply does whatever comes to be done and stays at ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Everything done is done by body, mind and senses with the ego; the Self is beyond them. While one lives in a body, some activity such as eating and sleeping continues, and he does it unattached. Cites Gita 3.8.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Objection: if all action stops, the body will die. Reply: what body and senses do is not done by the Self. Seeing this, the wise eat, drink and act free of ego, and stay in their blissful nature.

practical_reading: A way of working: do what is in front of you, fully, without the extra weight of 'I must be the one who achieves this'.
misreadings: Not drifting without plans or commitments
Not denying responsibility for what one does
speaks_to: New parents doing endless small tasks
not_for: Someone avoiding accountability

translation_note: Accurate.
context: This opens chapter 15, 'Knowledge of the Self', where Ashtavakra repeats the core teaching to steady Janaka. Verse 15.2 then compresses the whole teaching into one line.

key_terms.sense: instruction given in whatever casual way

core_teaching: A clear intellect is fulfilled by even a casual teaching, while an unprepared one stays confused despite a lifetime of inquiry.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Self-knowledge dawns at once on an intellect purified by discipline and the four qualifications (discernment, dispassion, the six virtues, longing for freedom). A ready disciple needs little instruction; the unready misconceive the Self however long they inquire.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Three grades of aspirant: the best awakens on hearing the great saying once, the middling through repeated hearing and reflection, the lowest after long study and worship. He cites Virochana, taught repeatedly without understanding.

practical_reading: It suggests shifting from collecting teachings to preparing the mind through honesty, calm and sincerity, so that simple truths can land.
misreadings: Not that some people are hopeless
Not anti-study; it is about readiness
cautions: Can make a long-time seeker feel inferior ('a muddled mind'); frame it as readiness that grows
speaks_to: Seekers who have read everything and feel stuck
Someone overloaded with courses and books
not_for: Someone who already feels stupid or inadequate

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 15.2 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: In chapter 15, right after saying a pure mind needs little teaching (15.1), Ashtavakra gives the teaching in one line. Verse 15.3 says this knowledge makes the talkative silent and the busy idle, which is why pleasure-seekers avoid it.
core_teaching: Liberation is losing the relish for sense-objects; bondage is relishing them. That is all there is to know, and the rest is up to you.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ashtavakra describes the essence of bondage and liberation in a few words and points to the aspirant's one duty. He cross-refers 10.4 (bondage is craving alone).

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: He quotes the saying that the mind alone causes bondage and liberation: attached to objects it binds, free of them it liberates. Having understood this much, do as you wish.

practical_reading: A simple self-test: where am I still savouring what hooks me? 'Do as you wish' hands the responsibility back to the student.
misreadings: 'Do as you wish' is not licence; it assumes the relish is already gone
Not hatred of the senses
speaks_to: Someone wanting a clear, compact teaching
not_for: Someone who might take 'do as you wish' as permission for harmful behaviour

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 15.4 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Translation accurate. The line adds 'your achievements', which is not in the verse (it says doer and enjoyer).
context: In chapter 15, after noting that pleasure-seekers avoid this knowledge (15.3), Ashtavakra restates the witness teaching. Verse 15.5 extends it to likes and dislikes.

key_terms.term: na tvaṃ deho na te dehaḥ
key_terms.sense: you are not the body, nor is the body yours

core_teaching: You are not the body or its owner, neither doer nor enjoyer, but consciousness: the ever-present witness that needs nothing. Live freely.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: A brief note: 'free' (nirapekṣa) means not depending on or conditioned by anything.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Doership and enjoyership belong to the mind, which you witness. Image: a lamp in a dance hall lights host, audience and dancer alike; the body is the hall, ego the host, intellect the dancer, consciousness the lamp.

practical_reading: For identity shaped by body image or performance, notice that you are the awareness in which body, deeds and results appear.
misreadings: Not neglect of the body or health
Not that your actions don't matter
cautions: 'Not your body' can sound like rejecting the body to someone with body-image distress or dissociation
not_for: Dissociation
Eating disorders, if it encourages ignoring the body

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 15.5 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: This chapter 15 verse follows 15.4 (not the body, not the doer). Next, 15.6 says to see the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.

key_terms.sense: free of mental constructs and conflict

core_teaching: Attraction and aversion belong to the mind, and the mind is never you. You are changeless awareness, so live freely.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The aspirant should neither love nor hate in the narrow, selfish sense, since that means identifying with the mind. He adds that universal love, which grows from true self-knowledge, is not what is to be dropped.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Friend, enemy and stranger are all distinctions of the mind. Attraction and aversion cannot be the Self's nature, since scripture calls the Self attributeless; if they were natural to it, liberation would be impossible.

practical_reading: It creates space around reactive likes and dislikes: notice 'I don't like this' as a passing mental event, not who you are.
misreadings: Not suppression of feelings
Nityaswarupananda explicitly says universal love is not what is meant to be dropped
speaks_to: Reactivity, irritability, strong dislikes of people
Someone who confuses their moods with their identity
not_for: Someone told their legitimate anger at injustice is 'just the mind'

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 15.8 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Translation accurate. Sanskrit typo: our text has 'नात्र मोऽहं'; it should be 'नात्र मोहं' (delusion), as in Nityaswarupananda and Jalim Singh. As written, 'मोऽहं' reads like 'so 'ham' and changes the sense.
context: In chapter 15, after the ocean image (15.7), Ashtavakra presses Janaka with repeated encouragement. Verses 15.9–10 then apply this to the body's coming and going.
core_teaching: An insistent call to trust that you are knowledge itself, the Lord, beyond nature, and not to slip back into confusion.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ashtavakra is impressing the Self's nature on the disciple. Until it is realised, one finds it hard to believe that the Self is what the sages say; 'beyond nature' means unaffected by it and controlling it.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Don't fall into the twin errors of doubting and misconceiving your conscious nature. He defines consciousness as self-luminous, lighting other things without needing anything else, and contrasts it with inert objects that know neither themselves nor others.

practical_reading: A reassurance when doubt creeps in: you are more than what is happening to you.
misreadings: Not 'you are God' in an egoistic sense
Not blind belief; śraddhā here is trust in the teaching while understanding matures
speaks_to: Someone who has lost faith in themselves
not_for: Someone in grandiosity

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 15.9 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Acceptable. 'Made of nature's qualities' takes guṇāḥ as the qualities of prakṛti and saṃveṣṭita as 'made of'. All three translators read guṇāḥ here as the senses, and saṃveṣṭita means 'wrapped in' ('the body with its senses').
context: In chapter 15, after urging faith (15.8), Ashtavakra applies the teaching to the body. Verse 15.10 continues: let the body last an aeon or end today.

key_terms.sense: wrapped in the guṇas; commentators read this as 'with the senses'

core_teaching: The body with its senses comes, stays and goes; the Self neither comes nor goes. So why mourn?

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self does not share the body's nature: the body changes and the Self does not. 'It' refers to the body's changes, such as death. He cites Gita 2.13 and 2.18.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The subtle body with its senses stays here, goes to other worlds and returns; the all-pervading Self, like space in a moving pot, never goes or comes. Don't grieve by attributing the body's birth and death to the Self.

practical_reading: Later in grief, or with fear of death, it can offer perspective: something in you, and in the one you love, is not subject to coming and going.
misreadings: Not a rule against mourning
Not 'the person who died doesn't matter'
cautions: It directly questions grieving; never use on Day 1 of a grief plan
Jalim Singh's reading relies on rebirth (the subtle body travelling to other worlds), which can feel dismissive in fresh grief
speaks_to: Later stages of grief seeking meaning
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Child loss
Suicidal ideation

translation_note: Translation accurate. The line's 'a hundred years' replaces kalpānta ('till the end of the cosmic age'); fine as paraphrase.

key_terms.sense: the end of a cosmic age
let it go this very day

core_teaching: Whether the body lasts till the end of the age or ends today, pure consciousness gains or loses nothing.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The body's conditions make not the slightest difference to the Self, so do not fear death. He cites Vivekachudamani 560–564 and Gita 2.17.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The seer is distinct from the seen: the body is seen and you are the seer. Whether it lasts an aeon or falls now, you neither persist nor perish with it, since you are what lends it existence.

practical_reading: With fears about health and mortality, it reminds you that your worth and being are not measured by lifespan.
misreadings: Not indifference to health or life
Not 'it doesn't matter if I die'
cautions: 'Let it go even today' must never reach someone with suicidal thoughts
speaks_to: Reflective people facing old age or illness with some steadiness
not_for: Suicidal ideation or self-harm
Fresh bereavement
The first days after a terminal diagnosis

translation_note: Accurate.
context: In chapter 15, after the body (15.10), the whole universe rises and falls like waves in the ocean that you are. Verse 15.12 adds that nothing is separate from you, so what is there to accept or reject?
core_teaching: In you, the boundless ocean, the world's waves rise and fall by their own nature; they neither add to you nor take away from you.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: 15.10 taught letting go of the body; this verse, of the universe. Creation and dissolution happen in time; the Self is beyond time. As waves neither add to nor subtract from the ocean, the universe adds nothing to the Self.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Your nature is an infinite ocean of consciousness, and the world-wave arises from ignorance and karma. Rising or setting, it brings you no loss or gain, since something imagined cannot harm its ground.

practical_reading: In turbulent times, events are waves; you can let them move without being diminished.
misreadings: Not indifference to world events or to others' suffering
cautions: The 'imagined world' framing (Jalim Singh) can feel dismissive during a collective tragedy
not_for: Fresh personal tragedy

translation_note: Accurate. The vocative cinmaya ('O you who are consciousness') is omitted, which is fine.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Be free of affirmations and negations, ideas such as 'I shall do this' and 'I shall not do this'.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: O conscious one, don't disturb your mind with willing and doubting. Free of them, abide in your own blissful nature.

practical_reading: For decision paralysis and second-guessing: make the decision, then stop re-arguing it in your head.
misreadings: Not avoiding decisions
Not forcibly suppressing thought
not_for: Someone who urgently needs to make a safety decision, if read as 'stop thinking'

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 16.1 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
translation_note: Narrowed. The Sanskrit says no abiding in oneself 'without forgetting everything' (sarvavismaraṇāt ṛte). Our translation ('until you forget them all') and line ('set them all down') limit 'all' to the scriptures. Nityaswarupananda and Richards both have 'forget all / everything'. Suggest: 'you will not be at ease until you forget everything.'
context: This opens chapter 16, 'Special instruction'. Verse 16.2 says that whether you enjoy, work or meditate, your mind will still long for the state beyond all desire. Verse 16.11 repeats the refrain: even with Shiva, Vishnu or Brahma as teacher, there is no ease without forgetting all.
core_teaching: However much scripture one recites or hears, one does not rest in the Self until everything, every mental construction, is forgotten.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Self-knowledge is experience, not intellect; scripture says the Self isn't gained by speech, intellect or Veda study. 'Forget all' means being conscious of the Self alone and seeing everything as the Self, not a deep-sleep blankness.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Quoting the Panchadashi: study and reflect, then drop the texts as a grain-seeker drops straw. Objection: in deep sleep all is forgotten, yet no one is freed. Reply: ignorance remains in sleep; the liberated forget ignorance too.

practical_reading: After study, let the concepts go and live from what you have understood.
misreadings: Not anti-learning or anti-scripture
Not mental blankness, and not forgetting responsibilities
cautions: In a scripture app, 'forget the scriptures' needs framing: study first, then go beyond concepts
speaks_to: People who intellectualise their inner life
not_for: Someone with memory loss or dementia, if read literally as 'forget everything'

translation_note: Accurate.
context: In chapter 16, verse 16.8 contrasted attachment to objects with aversion to them and said both bind. Here the attached person wants to flee the world; 16.10 then targets spiritual pride.

key_terms.sense: out of the wish to get rid of pain

core_teaching: The attached person wants to escape the world in order to escape pain. One free of attachment has no pain and is not distressed even while living in it.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The attached person thinks sorrow's cause lies in the world. But attachment to the world, not the world itself, is the root of misery; free of attachment one can live as happily in the world as anywhere.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The attached want to leave the world to escape the pain objects bring; the dispassionate are untroubled though the world continues. Quoting the Panchadashi: a tree with fire in its hollow can't turn green, nor an ignorant mind find peace.

practical_reading: It addresses 'geographical cures': changing job, city or partner won't fix an inner restlessness that travels with you.
misreadings: Not advice to stay somewhere harmful
Not against changing circumstances when that is needed
cautions: Must not be used to keep someone in an abusive relationship or an unsafe job
speaks_to: Someone who has changed jobs or cities repeatedly and still feels the same
not_for: Someone in danger who needs to leave

translation_note: Accurate.
context: In chapter 16, after 16.9 on fleeing the world, Ashtavakra targets spiritual pride. Verse 16.11 says that even a divine teacher cannot help without the forgetting of all.

key_terms.sense: one who only shares in suffering

core_teaching: Whoever is proud even of liberation, and still possessive about the body, is neither knower nor yogi, only a sufferer.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Abhimāna can mean egoism or conceit. Thinking 'I shall be free' or 'I am free' keeps the ego; pride in spiritual attainment is the opposite of knowledge. Claimed knowledge full of ego is a sad delusion that breeds misery.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha

core_teaching: The liberated one is at ease in every condition and the same everywhere; free of craving, he does not brood over what he has or hasn't done.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ego and its offspring, desire, come before every sense of action and duty. Free of them, the liberated soul is unconcerned with all his apparent actions, past, present and future.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The one liberated in life stays at ease in whatever situation prarabdha brings and is never anxious. He is content about deeds done and tasks ahead, insists on nothing, and so does not recall what was done or left undone.

practical_reading: For rumination and regret: once you have done what you can, including making amends, stop replaying the tape.
misreadings: Not a way to dodge accountability
Not forgetting the lessons learned
cautions: For someone who has harmed others, 'don't dwell on what you did' must be paired with making amends
not_for: Someone avoiding facing harm they caused
research_note: No classical Sanskrit bhashya by a major acharya is available; Vishveshvara's tika exists but its online OCR is unreadable. Commentary here is from Nityaswarupananda's 1940 notes (Ambuda proofing text) and Jalim Singh's 1903 Hindi tika (archive.org OCR), checked against Richards' translation. practical_reading is an editorial application drawn from these notes, not a quoted modern teacher.

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 18.99 (same numbering in Nityaswarupananda 1940, Jalim Singh 1903 and Richards 1994)
attribution_note: Setting's 'closing chapter' is inaccurate (18.100 ends the chapter; chapters 19–20 follow).
translation_note: Accurate.
context: This is the penultimate verse of chapter 18. Verse 18.100 closes it: the calm one runs neither to crowds nor to the forest and stays the same anywhere. Chapters 19–20 then give Janaka's final responses.
core_teaching: The free one is not elated by praise or angered by blame; he neither dreads death nor clings to life.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Being identified with the one absolute Self, there is for him no praiser or praise, no blamer or blame, and no life or death.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Praised, he doesn't rejoice; blamed, he isn't angry; facing death, he isn't afraid, since to him the Self is eternal and birth and death are nothing. He has no wish to live longer and no sorrow at dying.

practical_reading: The praise-and-blame half applies to work and social media. The life-and-death half suits people reflecting on mortality from a stable place.
misreadings: Not that life isn't worth living
Not indifference to others' opinions or feedback
cautions: 'Neither clings to life', and Jalim Singh's 'no wish to live longer', must not reach someone with suicidal thoughts
Mentions death
speaks_to: Reflecting on mortality in later life
not_for: Suicidal ideation
Fresh bereavement
